source.title: Achieving Margin Maximization Exponentially Fast via Progressive Norm Rescaling
source.authors: Mingze Wang; Ze-Ping Min; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies its proposed optimizer to non-separable data and a deep network, and reports test accuracy results. These results concern optimizer effects on generalization but do not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports theoretical and experimental margin-maximization results, but margin error is not the training-to-test gap named by the versions. The test-accuracy comparisons below are relevant to the broader claim's optimizer/generalization subject; no listed version covers PRGD.
record.test_reason: The study tests margin-maximization convergence and PRGD's test performance, but none of V1–V8. NGD here normalizes gradients by loss; it is not an Adam-like adaptive optimizer comparison testing V4. Margin error does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that PRGD accelerates margin maximization and report better test performance on Cancer and homogenized VGG-16/CIFAR-10 beyond their theory's scope. They propose applications to state-of-the-art models and combinations with explicit regularization as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes progressive norm rescaling (PRGD) and compares it with GD and NGD; it does not reproduce the listed studies' methods. Its deep-network test uses a homogenized VGG-16 without explicit regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-accuracy outcomes differ by dataset and training algorithm; no broader setting sweep for these results is described.

fits_no_version.finding: Best test accuracy on Cancer is 92.27% for PRGD versus 91.21% for both GD and NGD; on homogenized VGG-16/CIFAR-10 it is 89.29% versus 86.61% and 86.35%, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PRGD improves reported best test accuracy over GD and loss-normalized GD in these two experimental settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The theory establishes exponential directional and margin convergence for PRGD under stated separability and nondegeneracy assumptions; experiments demonstrate faster margin convergence on synthetic and digit datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressive norm rescaling can accelerate margin maximization relative to GD and NGD.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235 (2024)
record.problems: The test-accuracy section reports best test accuracy without uncertainty estimates or corresponding training accuracy, so the train-test gap cannot be assessed. The VGG result is for one architecture and dataset; the authors describe it as beyond the scope of their theory.
record.rows_left_out: Margin-maximization rates and margin errors in Sections 4, 7.1, and Appendix E concern margin convergence rather than the listed versions' training-to-test gap. No other test-accuracy outcomes are stated separately in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Matched random-label memorization and natural-label generalization experiments, including random-label held-out accuracy.
Width variation beyond the zero-training-error threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay under augmentation. Appendix E.2 mentions dropout but provides no intervention comparison.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and subsequent test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: Section 7.2 and Appendix E.2 contradict each other about explicit regularization; the actual VGG recipe cannot be resolved from this text. Missing training accuracy prevents assessing generalization gaps, but that alone is not why these results fail to test V1–V8: the required interventions and comparisons are absent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; the random-label control.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error across widths.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, including tuning and weight-decay conditions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their effect across training-set sizes or with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.note: Comparator for the reported PRGD result; no training accuracy or train-test gap is given.
rows.check: The 91.21% value matches Figure 5a, but this is a comparator in the proposed method's performance evaluation, not evidence for a listed version.

rows.subject: VGG-16

rows.note: Comparator for the reported PRGD result; no training accuracy or train-test gap is given.
rows.check: The 86.61% value matches Figure 5b. The no-explicit-regularization condition conflicts with Appendix E.2, which specifies classifier dropout and weight decay of 5×10^-4. Appendix E.2 also specifies momentum 0.9. This is a method-performance comparator.
